::: {.hidden}
$$
\newcommand{\expr}[3]{\begin{array}{c}
#1 \\
\bbox[lightblue,5px]{#2}
\end{array} ⊢ #3}
\newcommand{\ct}[1]{\bbox[font-size: 0.8em]{\mathsf{#1}}}

\def\true{\ct{T}}

Transitive verbs like *saw* increase the number of syntactic and semantic arguments of intransitives by one.
To analyze the sentence in (@ex-saw),

(@ex-saw) Sam saw Frodo.

we can assign a lexical entry like the one in (@ex-lexicon) to this verb.

(@ex-lexicon) $⟨\textit{saw}, (λx.(λy.\ct{see}(y, x)))⟩ ⊢ ((np\backslash s)/np)$

In this case, we have a function of the following type:

$$(λx.(λy.\ct{see}(y, x))) : (e → (e → t))$$

This function is defined in terms of a relation on entities, $\ct{see}$.
That is, given two entities $x$ and $y$, $\ct{see}(y, x)$ is some truth value.

Then, given the lexical entry for *Sam* on which its interpretation is $\ct{s}$, we can derive the meaning and syntactic category of the sentence in (@ex-saw):

$$\begin{prooftree}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{Sam}, \ct{s}⟩ ⊢ np\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{saw}, (λx.(λy.\ct{see}(y, x)))⟩ ⊢ (np\backslash s)/np\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{Frodo}, \ct{f}⟩ ⊢ np\)}
\RightLabel{\(/\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{saw Frodo}, (λx.(λy.\ct{see}(y, x)))(\ct{f})⟩ ⊢ (np\backslash s)\)}
\RightLabel{\(\backslash\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{Sam saw Frodo}, (λx.(λy.\ct{see}(y, x)))(\ct{f})(\ct{s})⟩ ⊢ s\)}
\end{prooftree}$$

Since $(λx.(λy.\ct{see}(y, x)))$ takes two entities in order, we can obtain a function that takes *one* entity by applying it first to $\ct{f}$:

$$(λx.(λy.\ct{see}(y, x)))(\ct{f})$$
$$⇒ (λy.\ct{see}(y, \ct{f}))$$

The resulting function is a characteristic function of a set of entities.
Thus if we apply the original function to *two* entities, we get a truth value:

$$(λx.(λy.\ct{see}(y, x)))(\ct{f})(\ct{s})$$
$$⇒ (λy.\ct{see}(y, \ct{f}))(\ct{s})$$
$$⇒ \ct{see}(\ct{s}, \ct{f})$$

This result, $\ct{see}(\ct{s}, \ct{f})$, will be $\true$ or $\false$, depending on the model.
